title: A field in wartime (Jeremiah 32:6–15)
hook: with the enemy at the gates, Jeremiah buys land: houses will be bought here again

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new covenant, and your line was on the heart. Did your words stay with you? Day four hundred seventy-seven.

Imagine a real estate agent calling you during a war. The enemy army is camped around your city. Siege ramps are going up against the walls. Food is running out. Everyone knows how this ends. And the agent says: there's a field for sale, just outside town. Actually, it's behind enemy lines right now. Interested? You'd hang up. Jeremiah didn't. He was under arrest at the time, held in the guard's courtyard of the king's palace, because he'd been saying out loud that Babylon would win. And his cousin came to see him with exactly that offer. Today, the strangest purchase in the Bible.
screen: `A CITY UNDER SIEGE.` → `JEREMIAH UNDER ARREST.` → `A FIELD FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: It's the tenth year of King Zedekiah. The Babylonian army surrounds Jerusalem. Jeremiah's cousin Hanameel comes and says: buy my field at Anathoth, our home village; the right to redeem it is yours. In Israel's law, when family land was about to be lost, a close relative had the right, and the duty, to buy it back so it stayed in the family. And God had told Jeremiah this visit was coming. So Jeremiah does it, and he does it properly. He weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. He signs the deed. He calls witnesses. He makes two copies, one sealed and one open, and hands them to his scribe, Baruch. Then he tells Baruch to put both in a clay jar, so they'll last a long time. Why the clay jar? Because he isn't buying for this year. He's buying for after. And then he says why, in the King James Bible: "For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land." This is the same prophet who has been warning for decades that the city will fall. He hasn't changed his message. He still says the city will fall. But he puts his money on the far side of the fall. And the next thing he does is pray, and in the prayer he admits it seems absurd: the city is being handed to the Chaldeans, and you told me to buy a field. He begins with: "Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee." Hope, here, isn't a feeling. It's a signed deed in a clay jar.
screen: `THE ARMY AT THE WALLS.` · `THE RIGHT TO REDEEM IS YOURS.` · `SEVENTEEN SHEKELS, A DEED, A JAR.` · `HOPE AS A SIGNED DEED.` · then, large: `FIELDS SHALL BE POSSESSED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one hopeful investment. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your world that feels besieged: your health, your town, a relationship, the news. Don't pretend it's fine. Jeremiah didn't. Then ask: what small thing could I put on the far side of this? A tree you could plant. A garden bed for next spring. A class you could sign up for. A letter to your future self. A friendship you could invest in. Picture yourself signing the deed. If you pray, you can offer that hope to God, the way Jeremiah did. The bell holds the time.
A field in wartime. Jeremiah's purchase under siege: seventeen shekels and a sealed deed in a clay jar, a bet on the far side of the fall.
Your line: houses will be bought again. Today, make one hopeful investment, small and concrete, in a future you can't see yet. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to Jeremiah 32 in times of crisis as a picture of hope that acts, and preachers have used it in wartime, in economic downturns and when churches build or plant in struggling neighborhoods.

fork.setup: you're Jeremiah, under arrest, with the enemy at the walls. your cousin offers to sell you the family field. what do you do?
options: refuse: the land is about to be lost anyway.
buy it, properly, and seal the deed in a clay jar.
promise to buy it after the war.
fork.reveal: he buys it, with witnesses and a sealed deed: "houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land."

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a prophet making a strange real estate deal.
what it means: hope that acts. Jeremiah buys land under siege as a sign that life will return after the fall.

what a scholar hears: a family redemption under the law of Leviticus 25, with a sealed and an open copy of the deed. a clay seal naming Berechiah son of Neriah the scribe has surfaced, though its authenticity is debated.

sources.quoted: For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee

notes: Hanameel is 'the son of Shallum thine uncle' (32:7), i.e. Jeremiah's cousin. Confirm.
Jeremiah was 'shut up in the court of the prison' in the king's house (32:2); 'guard's courtyard' in the voice. Confirm.
Bullae reading 'Berechyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' (Baruch's full name) appeared on the antiquities market; authenticity is disputed. Stated as debated. Keeper may prefer to drop.
KJV 32:17 wording: confirm exact text (by thy great power and stretched out arm).
